content.thinking:
I'm picturing a whimsical barnstormer biplane design, about 7m long with an 8m wingspan, featuring a chubby fuselage, round engine cowl, big propeller, rounded wings, cheerful cream/red/teal/yellow colors, and a scarfed pilot with bunting decorations. I'm planning the build carefully, keeping joints safe for the root and propeller components.

Mapping out the skeleton with a root body joint, wheel placement for ground clearance, and a hinged propeller joint at the nose. Working through the math for rotating and mirroring propeller blade shapes so they sweep symmetrically around the hub.

Writing fuselage loft stations...

Writing fuselage paint logic...

Shaping the wings as an extruded outline in the X-Z plane, thin along the Y-axis, with a rounded tip profile spanning about 8 units wide and 1.3 chord depth.

I'm positioning the top wing and bottom wing relative to the fuselage, with roughly 1.4 units of gap for struts to connect them.

Now I'm working out the ailerons as separate hinged parts on the wing trailing edges, defining their joints and outline geometry so they can rotate independently, and I'll color them red where they meet the main wing's trimmed trailing edge.

Still working out aileron outline coordinates and hinge orientation... I'm also noting that dihedral and sweep can be skipped for simplicity, and planning paired interplane struts on each side using rod elements.

Now I'm adding bracing wires as thin diagonal rods between the struts for visual charm, plus cabane struts connecting the fuselage top to the upper wing — specifying explicit bone attachments so each rod anchors correctly to the body or wing.

For the tail, I'm working out the fin's orientation and extrusion plane, computing cross products to get the thickness direction right, then sketching the fin outline as a set of 2D points along the fuselage's rear section, adjusting the anchor point and coordinates to get the leading edge sloping back toward the tail properly.

Still working through the geometry...

Checking fin base positioning against the fuselage geometry, it lines up correctly. Now I'm positioning the horizontal tailplane stabilizer in the XZ plane near the tail.

Still writing geometry outlines...

I realize the rudder and elevator overlap near the fuselage top at z=-3.0, so I need to check the tail fuselage height there and adjust the stabilizer y-position down to around 1.36 to match, fixing both the stab and rudder/fin base accordingly.

Now I'm designing the tail wheel setup with a small tire and strut, plus the main landing gear: large wheels on either side with V-strut supports, torus-shaped tires oriented along the x-axis, and cylindrical hubs with hubcap covers.

For the wheel discs, I'm layering concentric cylinders in cream, red, and yellow to mimic painted fabric-covered wheels, sizing the torus tire so its outer edge sits flush with the ground. Now I'm working out where to place open cockpits on the fuselage, planning to use dark cylinder shapes to suggest hollow cockpit openings behind the engine.

I'm adding a leather rim and dark recessed interior to the cockpits, then populating them whimsically — a goggled pilot with helmet and streaming scarf in the rear seat, and a small bear passenger up front — while calculating the fuselage's elliptical cross-section height at each cockpit's z-position so the openings sit correctly along the curved top.

Now I'm placing a small headrest hump behind the pilot and sketching translucent pale-blue windscreens in front of each cockpit opening, positioning them relative to the cowl and fuselage boundaries before moving on to the engine cowl detail.

For the radial engine look, I'm arranging nine small gray cylinder "rocker covers" in a ring around the front cowl face using trigonometric positioning, then considering hollowing out the cowl face instead of keeping it solid.

I'm adding a dark intake torus and nose disc at the cowl front, keeping the spinner sphere small enough to avoid colliding with the cylinder ring, then building two curved exhaust pipes along the fuselage sides using swept catmull curves with dark metal flared ends. Now I'm starting the propeller joint placement.

For the propeller, I'm defining a hinge joint at the nose with tapered wooden blades sized for a chunky silhouette, using a paint function that gives yellow tips over wood-colored bodies, and sizing the diameter so the lowest blade point still clears the ground. I'm also sketching out a whimsical bunting of triangular flags strung along a catenary rope between the wing struts for decoration.

Now I'm working out the actual rope path: running it from each wing tip down to the top of the tail fin with a natural sag, then spacing roughly a dozen small flag cards along that curve using frames derived from the path's tangent so each flag hangs correctly oriented.

I'm reconsidering the bunting path, maybe running it from the wing tips to the tail fin instead, accepting that the flag cards will appear at a slight oblique angle given the diagonal route.

For flags, I'm using a triangular SVG texture that hangs downward from the rope, with the card's bottom edge resting against the frame and extending along the lean direction.

Now I'm thinking through decal placement — adding a roundel number on the fuselage sides and wings using svg decals mapped onto the fuselage sweep surface.

Planning text decals too, maybe a small banner reading "BISCUIT" on the fuselage, accepting font-rendering risk. For the wings, I'm calculating exact y-offsets for upper and lower wing surfaces so roundel planes sit just above each wing's top face without clipping.

I'm also considering adding a painted leading-edge rod along the wing span, maybe wing-tip details or a wing walker figure for barnstormer flavor, but deciding to skip trailing banners and tip caps to keep complexity manageable, settling on bunting as sufficient decoration.

For the lower wing I'm defining its root attachment and chord outline, then working out strut placement between the wings—picking two bays per side with front and rear struts using rounded rod sections, plus diagonal wire bracing connecting the strut bases to the upper attachment points for that classic biplane rigging look.

I'm also planning cabane struts linking the fuselage to the upper wing root, and sketching cowl surface detail like small louver boxes arranged around the cowl's sides for that mechanical texture.

Now I'm positioning rows of tiny rivet spheres along the cowl's seam rim, spacing them in a ring to simulate panel fasteners.

For efficiency I'm merging the rivet spheres into a single geometry using BufferGeometryUtils, with a small helper function to place them along given point sets. For the fuselage seams I'm deciding to skip complex surface-loop helpers and instead approximate panel lines more simply, maybe through decals or painted stripes rather than true geometry.

Writing panel-line paint logic... Now I'm adding the pilot figure in the rear cockpit: a torso sphere, a head sphere with pink-tan skin tone, and a partial helmet sphere positioned above.

Adding goggles pushed up with a headband torus, lens cylinders in light blue, plus a nose and a whimsical oversized curly mustache for character.

I'm sweeping a long red and yellow striped scarf trailing from the neck behind the head, flaring and tapering as it flows over the headrest hump toward the back.

For the arms, I'm using capsules from shoulders to a control stick, with the hand gripping it as spheres for gloves. I'll skip extra joints for the pilot since only vehicle hinges matter, then add a small bear passenger in the front cockpit with spheres for the head, ears, muzzle, nose, and eyes, plus a tiny cap. Finally I'm building torus-shaped coaming rims around both cockpit openings, stretched along the z-axis to fit the fuselage shape.

For the cockpit interior, I'm figuring out how the torus and cylinder shapes orient so the stretching lines up correctly with the fuselage, then adding a dark disc for the cockpit hole and a small red headrest hump behind the pilot's seat.

Thinking about part count, I'm planning to aim for roughly 250 pieces total, adding wing details like aileron hinges and nav lights with a glow effect at the tips, plus considering some whimsical touches like fabric patches on the fuselage, though I'm skipping ideas like a horseshoe charm as too much.

Now I'm working out how to place decal patches on the fuselage surface, figuring out the geometry of where the fuselage curves at different stations and how the decal projection direction and anchor point need to align with the surface so the patch sits correctly without floating or clipping.

I'm reasoning through which way the decal text should face depending on which side of the aircraft the viewer sees, since mirroring the orientation on the opposite side is needed for the text to read correctly rather than appear backwards.

Given the mirroring complexity, I decide to avoid text altogether and go with symmetric graphics instead — a roundel and a cheerful winged emblem that look the same from either side.

Writing SVG decal code...

Defining paint colors and wing details...

I'm adding a teal cowl band, striped tail markings on the rudder/fin/stabilizer using red, cream and teal, plus a small pennant flag mounted on the fin top. Then I'm sketching out the joint hierarchy—body as root, with hinge joints for the prop, ailerons, rudder, elevators, and wheels—making sure each joint explicitly declares its parent.

I'm also defining a helper function to simplify attaching parts to bones with position and options, and double-checking that joint positions use the "at" override correctly for things like the spinner sphere on the propeller. Now I'm working through which imports are actually needed (createBuilder, frame, rng, catmull, paint, svg, toon helpers like cel/zigzag/INK, glow, mergeGeometries) to avoid unused-import errors, since I can't run a type checker to verify.

Setting up color palette...

Writing fuselage paint function...

Defining fuselage stations...

Working out the cowl radius and matching it with the fuselage curve path. I'm planning the lathe geometry for the engine cowl and spinner, positioning the propeller blades just outside the spinner radius, then sizing the cylinder head ring around the cowl face.

Now I'm setting up the nine cylinder heads, the gold intake ring torus, and the paint function that bands the cowl in teal and yellow stripes against red. I'm also placing a ring of rivet spheres and planning louvre vents along the fuselage sides.

Moving on, I'm designing the exhaust pipes as swept tubes along a curved path tucked just inside the cowl radius, tapering slightly with metal shading. Next I'm starting the windshield glass panels as tilted boxes angled back about 20 degrees.

Now I'm placing the cockpit rims and interior, then working out the bear's anatomy in detail: torso, head, ears, muzzle, nose, and eyes positioned relative to the head center, plus a small aviator cap as a partial hemisphere on top of the head.

Next I'm adding goggles with brass lens rings, paws resting on the coaming, and short arm capsules, then switching to the pilot figure—torso, head, leather helmet with ear flaps, and brass goggle lenses positioned on the front of the helmet using surface geometry calculations.

Now I'm placing the goggle lens details, a strap torus around the head, a small pink nose sphere, and curling mustache points using coordinate arrays near the pilot's face.

I'll skip the mouth, add rosy cheek spheres under the goggles, then add a flat yellow neck scarf torus and start sketching a catmull-rom streamer path trailing behind.

Still writing sweep geometry...

Now I'm adding capsule arms in leather tone with cream hand spheres, plus a control stick rod positioned between them.

I'm placing a scaled sphere as a headrest hump behind the pilot in bone-colored material, then starting to define the wing outlines with coordinate points for the upper wing panel.

Defining aileron geometry...

Lower wing passes through the fuselage center, which should be fine. I'm checking strut attachment points at x 1.6 and 3.0, confirming the lower wing chord geometry lines up at those positions with z around 0.6 to -0.1 for the strut heights.

Now I'm placing the roundel decals: upper wing roundels at x=±2.6 with a small offset above and below the wing surface to avoid z-fighting, sized at 0.9, and lower wing roundels smaller at 0.7 near x=±2.0. I'm also positioning wingtip navigation lights as small glowing spheres—red on the left, green on the right—near the wing tips, and sketching a leading-edge tube along the wing's front edge for visual detail.

I'm defining a helper function for struts that connects attachment points between the wings with thin rod geometry in a wood-toned color, plus small brass collar fittings at each joint, which I plan to merge into a single geometry for efficiency. I'm now laying out the strut and bracing wire positions across both wing bays, computing endpoint coordinates with slight outward lean for the upper attachments.

Next I'm working out the cabane struts connecting the fuselage to the upper wing, then moving to the landing gear—V-struts running from the fuselage down to the wheel hubs, an axle spanning between them, and tire geometry built from a torus shape in a dark rubber tone.

I'm layering wheel details next: a cream disc, a red ring, and a yellow cap stacked concentrically to create the wheel's painted face, checking that each layer's height and radius fits within the tire's outer profile. Then I work out the tail wheel assembly—joint position, tire cylinder, and support strut connecting it to the tail fuselage—before starting on the horizontal stabilizer placement, aligning its thickness with the tapered tail section.

Working out the elevator, fin, and rudder outlines...

I'm defining the rudder's striped paint pattern, the teal fin coloring, and a metal rod with a swallowtail pennant flag flying off the fin top. Now I'm plotting a catmull-rom bunting path connecting the tail decorations to the fin's leading edge geometry, checking the coordinates line up without crossing.

I'm setting up flag cards along the bunting path using frame sampling and attaching alternating flag textures, then writing the SVG template for the triangular flag shape with a colored circle emblem.

Now I'm sweeping a thin rope tube along the path for the bunting cord, then considering skipping a pitot tube detail and adding a fuselage emblem decal via a mirrored ray-cast on both sides.

Skipping roundels, fuel tanks, and harness details for now, I'm estimating the total part count will land around 150-200 after merges, which seems reasonable.

Now I'm handling null hits from the ray cast by skipping them, and setting up the decal options with position, direction, size, and up vector. For the propeller, I'm shaping the blade with a tapered extrude profile that's wider at the root and narrows toward the tip, with smoothing and a small bevel applied.

I'm coloring the blade with a paint function that applies yellow near the tip and a wood-grain pattern elsewhere, computing the two blade orientation vectors at 15° and 195° so their cross product confirms correct facing, and adding a small brass hub cylinder. I'm skipping extra details like fuel cap bolts and landing struts, moving toward assembling the final toy bear composition.

Now I'm defining a reusable wing-paint helper that colors most of the wing red but adds a dark non-slip walkway patch near the root on top of the lower wing, checking the point's x and z position and surface normal to decide where that patch applies.

Writing wing paint logic...

I'm figuring out rib tape placement using a modular distance calculation so thin tape stripes appear at regular intervals along the span, sized to about 3.4cm wide, then capping the wingtip colors (red beyond x=3.6 upper, 3.0 lower) and deciding to skip extra fuselage checker decals and exhaust staining for now, keeping skin tones simple.

I'm sanity-checking proportions — wheel and tail wheel bottoms sit at floor level, overall length ~5.3m and wingspan 8.1m, smaller and chubbier than a real Stearman but fine for this stylized build. I confirm merging sphere geometries for strut ball joints and cowl rivets works since all share compatible position/normal/uv attributes, using a non-null merge helper and chained sphere translations for each strut end.

Now I'm setting up the joint structure, naming left/right sides by sign (L for positive X, R otherwise) for symmetric parts like ailerons that rotate about the x-axis. I'm working out a typed wrapper for part colors, settling on a union type combining string literals with the paint function's return type so I can call the part-placement helper concisely without importing extra context types.

Writing part helper function...

I decide to skip finer details like a leather seat interior and lathe smoothing on the cowl, since sharp creases above 35 degrees are fine as-is. Now I'm planning to write out mirrored loops for symmetric features like goggles, plus a texture-building function for the flag.

Designing emblem SVG graphics...

Now I'm reasoning through the pilot and bear geometry—partial sphere helmets with tilted rotation so the opening faces forward and exposes the face, plus goggle lens cylinders oriented along the correct axis. I'm confirming the rotation math checks out before finalizing and writing the file.
